title: Fewest Insertions for a Mirror Word
statement:
You get a lowercase string s. In one step you may insert any single letter at any position: the front, the back or between two letters.

Return the fewest insertions needed so that s reads the same forwards and backwards.

examples.why: No letter repeats, so only one letter can stay as the centre. Every other letter needs a partner: "mangognam".
Comparing s with its reverse gives many mismatched positions, but "racecar" is already a mirror. Put an "s" in front: "sracecars".

constraints: s holds only lowercase English letters
hints: Look at the first and last letters. If they match, what is left to solve? If they do not, one of them needs a new partner.
Let f(i, j) be the answer for the slice s[i..j]. Equal ends give f(i+1, j-1); otherwise 1 + min(f(i+1, j), f(i, j-1)).

Another view: letters that are already part of the longest mirrored subsequence stay; every other letter needs exactly one inserted partner. That subsequence is the longest common subsequence of s and its reverse.

explain.intuition:
Look at the two ends of the string. If they are the same letter, they already pair up and the problem shrinks to the inside. If they differ, one of them must get a new partner inserted on the other side. We do not know which choice is better, so try both and keep the cheaper one. Slices overlap heavily, so store each slice's answer in a table: that turns an exponential search into O(n²).

There is a neat second view. Some letters can stay as they are, forming a mirrored subsequence. Every other letter needs one inserted twin. So the answer is n − (longest mirrored subsequence), and the longest mirrored subsequence equals the longest common subsequence of s and reverse(s).
steps: Make a table dp[i][j] = fewest insertions for s[i..j]. Single letters and empty slices cost 0.
Fill it by slice length, shortest first, or loop i from right to left and j from i + 1 to the right.
Return dp[0][n-1]. Only row i + 1 is needed while filling row i, so one array is enough.
pitfalls: Counting mismatched positions between s and its reverse. In "racecars" that counts many mismatches, but one insertion is enough.
Greedily adding the letter that mismatches at the ends without trying the other side. "xabcbay" shows both choices must be compared.
Filling the table in the wrong order, so that dp[i+1][j-1] is read before it is computed.

solutions.title: Plain recursion on the ends
solutions.idea: Match equal ends, otherwise try giving a partner to the left or to the right letter. Exponential without a memo.

solutions.title: Interval DP with one row
solutions.idea: dp[j] holds the answer for s[i..j]. Walk i from the right; prev keeps the old dp[j-1], which is dp[i+1][j-1].

solutions.title: Length minus the longest mirrored subsequence
solutions.idea: The letters that can stay form the longest common subsequence of s and its reverse. Each other letter needs one twin.

followups: Return one shortest mirror word, not just the count. How do you walk back through the table?
Only insertions at the front are allowed. Which much faster technique fits then?
